3.3 Simulated Entry Condition
Criterion	Description	Why it’s chosen
Price above 50‑day moving average (MA)	Common trend‑following indicator.	Signals a short‑term uptrend.
RSI > 50	Relative Strength Index (RSI) above 50 indicates bullish momentum.	Filters out weak up‑moves.
Volume > 1.5× 20‑day average	Volume spike confirms participation.	Reduces chance of a false breakout.
Price > recent swing high	Must close above the last 10‑day high.	Confirms a new resistance level is being tested.
Entry trigger: All four conditions must be satisfied on the same trading day. A limit order would be placed at the next intraday high (e.g., ₹1,190) to avoid slippage.

4. Risk Management
Rule	Detail	Purpose
Stop‑loss	₹1,160.81 (2 % below entry)	Caps loss at ₹10,000 (1 % of equity).
Take‑profit	4 % above entry (≈ ₹1,218.78)	Targets a 2:1 reward‑to‑risk ratio.
Trailing stop	If price moves 1 % above entry, move stop‑loss to 1 % below new high	Locks in gains while allowing upside.
Maximum daily loss	₹20,000 (2 % of equity)	Prevents a single day from eroding too much capital.
Position limit	No more than 5 % of equity in any single stock	Diversifies risk across the portfolio.
Monitoring	Review trade status at least twice per day	Ensures stop‑loss and trailing stop are functioning.
5. Limitations and Conclusion
Limitations
Historical data only – All metrics are derived from past performance and do not predict future results.
Sample size – Volatility estimate is based on 126 daily observations (~6 months); a larger sample could yield a different figure.
No real‑time data – The execution plan uses hypothetical entry conditions; actual market dynamics may differ.
No fundamental analysis – The plan relies solely on technical signals; company fundamentals, macro events, and news are not incorporated.
Transaction costs – The illustrative cost calculation assumes flat fees and a 0.1 % commission; actual costs may vary.
Risk assumptions – The 1 % risk per trade and 2 % daily loss limits are illustrative; investors should adjust them to their own risk tolerance.
Conclusion
Using the available historical metrics, RELIANCE.NS could move into a bullish, sideways, or bearish trajectory. The direction will largely depend on how company fundamentals, macro conditions, and sector dynamics evolve relative to the current 6‑month decline and the 21 % annualized volatility benchmark.

The hypothetical execution plan demonstrates how a trader might structure a trade if the technical entry conditions are met, while the risk‑management rules ensure that potential losses are capped and gains are protected.

Investors should monitor earnings releases, macro indicators, and technical price action for signals that align with one of the three scenarios outlined above, and adjust their strategies accordingly.
